title: Dispensing and Administering Without an Individual Prescription: Opioid Antagonists, Standing Orders and Emergency Vaccine Orders
topic: Public health / Opioid antagonist access, the pharmacist standing-order regimes, and emergency vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order
subtopic: Prescribing and dispensing an opioid antagonist to a person at risk or a person in a position to assist under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(d); the statewide standing order, purchaser billing, dose reporting and good-faith protections in s. 19B; the over-the-counter and prescription naloxone distinction drawn by the Drug Control Program, the Department's guidance on open-shelf access to over-the-counter naloxone and the registration exemption in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(11); the pharmacy duties in 247 CMR 9.06 read with the Board's definition of dispensing, the continuous-supply provisos in s. 19C, and the Board's statewide stocking statement and naloxone reporting method in Policy 2024-01; the emergency contraception and COVID-19 standing orders in s. 19A(a)-(c) and s. 19E(a)-(b), the training contrast between s. 19A(d) and s. 19E(c) and the reporting provisions in s. 19A(e), s. 19B(d) and s. 19E(d); and emergency vaccine administration under 105 CMR 700.003(F) with the registration exemption in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(7)
learning_objectives: State to whom an opioid antagonist may lawfully be prescribed and dispensed under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(d), and how such a prescription is regarded for purposes of chapters 94C and 112.

Explain what the statewide standing orders in s. 19A and s. 19B authorize, who issues each and in what terms, and what each must include, and do the same for the standing order in s. 19E, including what a COVID-19 control measure covers.

Tell over-the-counter naloxone from prescription naloxone as the Drug Control Program's advisory does, by the FDA-approved packaging, and state what follows for the Program's regulations and for registration, including the exemption in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(11).
Apply s. 19B(e) to a purchase made for someone else: whose coverage is pursued, when the claim is submitted, and what changes when the purchaser asks to pay out-of-pocket.

Name the duties 247 CMR 9.06 places on a pharmacy, namely counseling and the opioid antagonist information pamphlet on dispensing, referral, continuous supply and the rescue kit label, state the event that triggers each, and explain why an ordinary over-the-counter sale is not dispensing.

State the two provisos M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C attaches to the continuous supply of opioid antagonists, explain the Board's statement in Policy 2024-01 that all areas of Massachusetts experience high incidences of opioid-related overdoses or deaths, and give the course that meets the statute, 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) and the Board's policy for any Massachusetts pharmacy.
Contrast the permissive emergency contraception training in s. 19A(d) with the mandatory COVID-19 drug training in s. 19E(c), and recognize that s. 19B states no training requirement.

Compare the reporting provisions in s. 19A(e), s. 19B(d) and s. 19E(d) by trigger, content, patient-identification language, confidentiality and public-records status, and describe how the Board's Policy 2024-01 has a pharmacy report naloxone doses.

Work through the Commissioner-side and practitioner-side conditions of 105 CMR 700.003(F), the student condition, the training, supervision and written-protocol duties in 105 CMR 700.003(F)(2), and the registration exemption in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(7).

State the good-faith protections in s. 19B for the dispensing pharmacist, the issuer of the standing order and prescribing or dispensing practitioners, and the person who administers an opioid antagonist, and the exception the first two carry.

orientation.text: An opioid antagonist can reach the person who may need it by more than one route, and several of them do not begin with a prescription written for that person. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(d) provides that naloxone or other opioid antagonist may lawfully be prescribed and dispensed to a person at risk of experiencing an opiate-related overdose or to a family member, friend or other person in a position to assist such a person, and that for purposes of chapters 94C and 112 any such prescription shall be regarded as being issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice. The person who collects the antagonist therefore need not be the person expected to overdose. Section 19B supplies a route that needs no individual prescription at all. The department shall ensure that a statewide standing order is issued to authorize the dispensing of an opioid antagonist in the Commonwealth by any licensed pharmacist; the Commissioner, or a physician designated by the Commissioner and registered under s. 7 to distribute or dispense a controlled substance in the course of professional practice, may issue it; and it shall include, but not be limited to, written, standardized procedures or protocols for the dispensing of an opioid antagonist by a licensed pharmacist. Under s. 19B(c) a licensed pharmacist may dispense an opioid antagonist in accordance with that order. The Board's regulation assumes the same two routes: 247 CMR 9.06(2)(b) allows a pharmacy that is not located in a high overdose area to dispense naloxone rescue kits or other approved opioid antagonists pursuant to the statewide standing order or a prescription, provided the pharmacy complies with all other provisions of 247 CMR 9.06, although, as explained below, the Board has stated that all areas of Massachusetts experience high incidences of opioid-related overdoses or deaths. Section 19B(a), and 247 CMR 9.06(1)(c) for the Board's regulation, define an opioid antagonist as naloxone or any other drug approved by the federal Food and Drug Administration as a competitive narcotic antagonist used in the reversal of overdoses caused by opioids. At the scene, s. 19B(g) provides that a person acting in good faith may receive a prescription for an opioid antagonist, possess an opioid antagonist, and administer it to an individual appearing to experience an opioid-related overdose. Separately, 105 CMR 700.004(B)(11) provides that no person shall be required to register with the Department for the purposes of purchasing, storing, possessing, or administering naloxone, or other opioid antagonist approved by the Department; that exemption speaks of an antagonist approved by the Department rather than using the federal-approval definition in s. 19B(a).

Naloxone on a pharmacy shelf and naloxone in the prescription department may be different legal products. The Drug Control Program's advisory on its regulations and over-the-counter naloxone explains that naloxone is currently available both as an over-the-counter medication and as a medication which cannot be dispensed without a prescription or standing order, that over-the-counter naloxone and prescription naloxone are separate and distinct products to which different laws and regulations apply, and that the two can be identified by reference to their packaging. Over-the-counter naloxone is sold in FDA-approved packaging for over-the-counter medications; prescription naloxone is sold in FDA-approved packaging which states that federal law prohibits dispensing without a prescription. The Program's regulations do not apply to activities regarding over-the-counter naloxone and do apply to activities regarding prescription naloxone, and a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration is not required for activities regarding the over-the-counter product. The counseling, pamphlet, referral, billing and reporting provisions taught below are written around dispensing an opioid antagonist, on a prescription or under the statewide standing order, and they do not address over-the-counter packages in terms. The continuous-supply statute, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C, by contrast provides expressly that the continuous supply shall include opioid antagonists approved to be sold over the counter without a prescription. The counseling and pamphlet duty in 247 CMR 9.06(3) falls on a pharmacy that dispenses, and 247 CMR 2.00 defines dispensing as the physical act of delivering a drug, chemical, device or combination thereof to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, including the use of the pharmacist's professional judgment and the packaging, labeling or compounding necessary to prepare it for delivery. An ordinary over-the-counter sale is made without any such order, so it is not dispensing in that sense, and the duty attaches when the pharmacy dispenses on a prescription or under the statewide standing order. Department guidance points the same way: the Department of Public Health's memorandum to Massachusetts retailers on over-the-counter naloxone, dated 12/20/2023, says that retailers should enable anonymous access to naloxone directly on a shelf, without locking it behind a cabinet or placing it in a container that requires contacting an employee to reach it.

When an opioid antagonist is dispensed under s. 19B, three sets of obligations meet at the counter, and they do not all fall on the same actor. The first is payment. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19B(e) a pharmacist or designee who dispenses an opioid antagonist pursuant to that section shall, for the purposes of health insurance billing and cost-sharing, treat the transaction as the dispensing of a prescription to the person purchasing the opioid antagonist, regardless of the ultimate user; and unless the purchaser requests to pay for the prescription out-of-pocket, the pharmacist or designee shall make a reasonable effort to identify the purchaser's insurance coverage and to submit a claim for the opioid antagonist to the insurance carrier prior to dispensing. The coverage pursued is the purchaser's, a purchase made for someone else is not thereby a cash sale, and the claim comes before the hand-over. The second is counseling and information, and the Board places it on the pharmacy: under 247 CMR 9.06(3) a pharmacy that dispenses a naloxone rescue kit or other approved opioid antagonist shall provide counseling and the opioid antagonist information pamphlet at the time of dispensing, the pamphlet being, under 247 CMR 9.06(1)(b), a Board-approved pamphlet that provides information about an opioid antagonist and responding to an overdose. Spoken counseling does not stand in for the pamphlet, because the regulation requires both. The third arises when there is nothing to dispense: under 247 CMR 9.06(4) a pharmacy that does not have a naloxone rescue kit or other approved opioid antagonist readily available for dispensing at the time requested shall refer the requestor to the nearest location that has one readily available. A stock-out therefore starts an obligation rather than ending one. The adverse-risk information and opioid antagonist offer under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18D, and the pamphlet under s. 21, which arise when certain controlled substances are dispensed, are a separate subject taught with the dispensing label and record.

Two further provisions of 247 CMR 9.06 concern the stock itself, and on them the Board's policy matters as much as the regulation's wording. A high overdose area is, under 247 CMR 9.06(1)(a), a geographical area that appears on a list published by the Board, in consultation with the Department of Public Health, of areas with high incidence of opiate overdose, and under 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) a pharmacy located in a high overdose area shall maintain a continuous supply of naloxone rescue kits or other approved opioid antagonists readily available for dispensing. Read alone, that wording suggests a line between pharmacies inside and outside listed areas, and 247 CMR 9.06(2)(b) speaks of a pharmacy that is not located in one. The Board's Policy 2024-01, Naloxone Dispensing (adopted 1/11/24, revised 2/6/25), answers the question the wording leaves open. It states that since all areas of Massachusetts experience high incidences of opioid-related overdoses or deaths, Massachusetts pharmacies are required to stock naloxone in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C, and that pharmacies must maintain a continuous, sufficient supply of naloxone to meet the needs of the community. The Board's retail compliance inspection report lists that statement as an item checked at inspection, citing 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) and (b) and the policy, and the statewide naloxone standing order signed July 13, 2026 refers to the policy for dispensing under the order. The policy is Board guidance rather than regulation and is not itself set out as a list of areas, but both 247 CMR 9.06(1)(a) and s. 19C leave the areas to the Board, in consultation with the Department, to identify; no Massachusetts pharmacy should treat its location as excusing it from keeping naloxone in stock, and the course that is safe on either reading, and the one the Board inspects against, is a continuous supply in every Massachusetts pharmacy. For such a pharmacy an empty shelf is a problem in its own right, and making the referral required by 247 CMR 9.06(4) does not supply the continuous stock that 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) and the Board's policy call for. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C adds two provisos that the text of 247 CMR 9.06 does not repeat. It provides that the Board shall promulgate regulations requiring pharmacies located in areas with high incidence of opiate overdose, as determined by the Board in consultation with the department, to maintain a continuous supply of opioid antagonists as defined in s. 19B; that the continuous supply shall include opioid antagonists approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration to be sold over the counter without a prescription; and that such pharmacies shall notify the department if the supply or stock of opioid antagonist doses is insufficient to enable compliance with maintaining a continuous supply. A Massachusetts pharmacy that keeps a continuous, sufficient supply of naloxone rescue kits or other approved opioid antagonists readily available for dispensing, includes over-the-counter antagonists in that supply, and notifies the department when its supply or stock of doses is insufficient to maintain it meets the words of the statute, the regulation and the Board's policy. Finally, under 247 CMR 9.06(5) a pharmacy that assembles opioid antagonist rescue kits shall affix a label to the outer package noting "Opioid Antagonist Rescue Kit" or the name of the opioid antagonist followed by "Rescue Kit", together with the expiration date, which shall be based on the expiration date of the included unit.

Section 19B also protects those who make the scheme work, and the protections are not identical. Under s. 19B(c), except for an act of gross negligence or willful misconduct, a pharmacist who, acting in good faith, dispenses an opioid antagonist shall not be subject to any criminal or civil liability or any professional disciplinary action by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy related to the use or administration of an opioid antagonist. Under s. 19B(f), on the same exception for gross negligence or willful misconduct, the Commissioner or a physician who issues the statewide standing order, and any practitioner who, acting in good faith, directly or through the standing order, prescribes or dispenses an opioid antagonist, shall not be subject to any criminal or civil liability or any professional disciplinary action. Under s. 19B(g) a person who, acting in good faith, administers an opioid antagonist to an individual appearing to experience an opioid-related overdose shall not, as a result of the person's acts or omissions, be subject to any criminal or civil liability or any professional disciplinary action, and the immunity established under s. 34A also applies to a person administering an opioid antagonist under s. 19B. That subsection states no exception for gross negligence or willful misconduct. Good faith is stated as a condition for the dispensing pharmacist, for the prescribing or dispensing practitioner and for the person who administers, and the pharmacist's protection is framed around liability and Board discipline related to the use or administration of the opioid antagonist.

This section compares three regimes in chapter 94C under which a pharmacist dispenses on a standing order rather than an individual prescription, and the orders themselves differ. Under s. 19A(a), emergency contraception means any drug approved by the federal Food and Drug Administration as a contraceptive method for use after sexual intercourse, whether provided over-the-counter or by prescription. Under s. 19A(b) the department shall ensure that a statewide standing order is issued to authorize the dispensing of emergency contraception by a licensed pharmacist; the order shall include, but not be limited to, written, standardized procedures or protocols for that dispensing; and the Commissioner, or a physician designated by the Commissioner who is registered to distribute or dispense a controlled substance in the course of professional practice pursuant to s. 7, shall issue it. Under s. 19A(c) a licensed pharmacist may dispense emergency contraception in accordance with that order. Section 19B(b) follows the same pattern for opioid antagonists, in that the department shall ensure the order is issued and the order shall include written, standardized procedures or protocols, but it provides that the Commissioner or designated physician may issue the order where s. 19A(b) says shall. Section 19E differs in both definition and issuer. Under s. 19E(a) a COVID-19 control measure means a COVID-19 drug, COVID-19 test or other COVID-19 diagnostic device approved or otherwise authorized by the federal Food and Drug Administration, and under s. 19E(b) the Commissioner, or an actively practicing physician who currently prescribes a COVID-19 drug, is designated by the Commissioner and is registered under s. 7 to prescribe or dispense a controlled substance in the course of professional practice, may issue a standing order that may be used for a licensed pharmacist to dispense a COVID-19 control measure. That order shall include, but not be limited to, written standardized procedures or protocols developed by the Commissioner in collaboration with an actively practicing physician who currently prescribes a COVID-19 drug, and those procedures and protocols shall be consistent with the Food and Drug Administration's revised Emergency Use Authorization for Paxlovid issued July 6, 2022 and declarations issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services under the federal Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness Act. Pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception under s. 19F is taught separately.

The training provisions point in different directions. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19A(d), before dispensing emergency contraception authorized under that section a pharmacist may complete a training program approved by the Commissioner on emergency contraception, and the permissive word governs whether the training is taken, not what it contains: the training shall include, but not be limited to, proper documentation, quality assurance and referral to additional services, including appropriate recommendation that the patient follow up with a medical practitioner. Under s. 19E(c) a pharmacist may dispense a COVID-19 control measure in accordance with a standing order issued under s. 19E(b), provided that before dispensing a COVID-19 drug the pharmacist shall complete a training program approved by the Commissioner on COVID-19 drugs, which shall include, but not be limited to, evaluation of the patient's medical history and relevant records including recent reports of laboratory blood work to review for kidney or liver problems, clinical considerations relative to contraindications with commonly prescribed medications, recommendations for clinical monitoring for side effects, and appropriate recommendation that the patient follow up with a medical practitioner. The proviso attaches the mandatory training to a COVID-19 drug and does not name tests or devices. The opioid antagonist regime has no training provision in s. 19B or in 247 CMR 9.06; what s. 19B(b) requires instead is that the standing order itself include written, standardized procedures or protocols for dispensing.

The statutory reporting provisions differ in trigger, in what is counted and in their confidentiality wording, and each is written for the dispensing pharmacist. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19A(e) a pharmacist dispensing emergency contraception under s. 19A shall annually provide to the department the number of times such emergency contraception is dispensed, and the reports shall not identify any individual patient, shall be confidential and shall not be public records as defined by clause Twenty-sixth of section 7 of chapter 4 or section 10 of chapter 66. Under s. 19B(d) a pharmacist who dispenses an opioid antagonist shall annually report to the department the number of opioid antagonist doses dispensed; the reports shall not identify an individual patient, shall be confidential and shall not constitute a public record as defined in clause Twenty-sixth of section 7 of chapter 4, and the department shall publish an annual report that includes aggregate information about the dispensing of opioid antagonists in the Commonwealth. Unlike s. 19A(e), which speaks of dispensing under s. 19A, and s. 19E(d), which speaks of dispensing in accordance with a standing order, the reporting sentence in s. 19B(d) is not limited in its terms to dispensing under s. 19B. Under s. 19E(d) a pharmacist who dispenses a COVID-19 control measure in accordance with a standing order issued under s. 19E(b) shall, upon request, report to the department on the doses, tests or devices dispensed; those reports shall be confidential and shall not constitute a public record under clause Twenty-sixth of section 7 of chapter 4, and the department shall publish an annual report with aggregate information about the dispensing of COVID-19 control measures. Section 19E(d) does not contain the sentence, found in s. 19A(e) and s. 19B(d), that reports shall not identify an individual patient, and s. 19A contains no provision for a published aggregate report. Two regimes report annually and one upon request, and in all three the reports are confidential and outside the public-records definition. For opioid antagonists the Board has also set out how the report is made. Its Policy 2024-01, citing s. 19B, states that each Massachusetts pharmacy must report the number of naloxone doses dispensed. The preferred method is the pharmacy's daily Prescription Monitoring Program submissions, which are for data collection only and do not appear on a patient's profile in the program; a pharmacy that chooses not to report that way must email an annual report by January 15 giving, for the previous calendar year, its name and zip code, the total number of naloxone doses dispensed, counted as doses rather than prescriptions or manufacturer-supplied units, and the number of those doses paid for with insurance, while details of each dispensing event are encouraged but not required.

Emergency vaccine administration under 105 CMR 700.003(F) works differently again, because it opens on a decision of the Commissioner rather than on a standing order for pharmacists. Notwithstanding any other Department regulation, a health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department, or a student duly enrolled in an approved or accredited program for licensure as a health care professional and acting in accordance with the policies of that program, may possess and administer any vaccine designated by the Commissioner for the prevention of a pandemic, novel, or other vaccine-preventable disease, provided the Commissioner determines that there are or will be insufficient health care professionals available for timely vaccine administration and issues an order authorizing such administration. The gate then has two parts, and 105 CMR 700.003(F)(1) requires both. On the Commissioner's side, the person must be authorized to administer vaccine by order of the Commissioner. On the practitioner's side, administration must be in accordance with the Commissioner's order and the order or prescription of a duly registered practitioner authorized to issue an order or prescription for a vaccine pursuant to 105 CMR 700.000. A practitioner's standing prescription does not open the pathway without the Commissioner's order, and the Commissioner's order does not dispense with the practitioner's order or prescription. A student must in addition be authorized and supervised by a licensed and qualified health care professional. Paragraph (F)(2) then governs how the work is done by a person administering vaccine, whether a licensed professional or a student: in accordance with the Commissioner's order, that person shall receive proper training and supervision in the administration of the vaccine, and shall comply with written protocols to ensure proper storage, handling and return of vaccine, recordkeeping regarding administration, response to adverse events, and safe and appropriate administration of vaccine. A person so authorized needs no separate registration for that work: under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(7), a health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department, or a student duly enrolled in an approved or accredited program for such licensure or certification, who is authorized by 105 CMR 700.003(F) to possess and administer vaccine is exempt from registration for purposes of administering vaccine pursuant to 105 CMR 700.003(F). Routine pharmacist administration, including immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) and the eligible list, route and dose for other medications, is taught in the section on what pharmacists and pharmacy interns may administer, and vaccine administration under collaborative drug therapy management is taught with collaborative practice.
